transcript:
Header: Date: 2027-08-21 11:00 AM PST | Duration: 58m | Attendees: Alex Morgan (Redwood AE), Priya Patel (Redwood SE), Samuel Lee (CTO - Nimbus), Maya Chen (Infra Lead), Daniel Ortiz (SecOps)

Summary: quick sync to walk through the private VPC topology options and the runtime-level implications for inference latency/throughput. Focus on PrivateLink vs TGW, egress/NAT constraints, DNS and resolver options, and how batching/KV cache and quantization change network behaviour.

[00:00] Alex: hey everyone, thanks for joining, uh we'll, we'll do a quick intro—Priya is our inference SE, she'll drive most of the technical stuff. Sam, Maya, Danny from Nimbus?
[00:10] Samuel: yeah hi, Sam here. thanks Alex. we've got two main asks: low single-digit 100s ms latency for customer-facing flows, and strict no-public-egress for secrets and PII.
[00:25] Priya: awesome, that's exactly what we wanted to validate. quick agenda: network topology options, where PrivateLink fits, egress/NAT constraints, DNS and resolver options, then runtime perf (kv cache, batching, quantization) and recommended pilot tests.
[00:40] Maya: just to flag, our infra team is on AWS, we prefer PrivateLink over opening wide egress, and we use centralized NAT gateways in a partner account.
[00:55] Priya: perfect, that's a common pattern. so first, PrivateLink: it gives you an interface endpoint inside your VPC so all traffic to Redwood control plane or runtime endpoints never traverses the public internet. you get stable private IPs and SG control. downside is throughput per ENI and you pay for endpoint hours/GB.
[01:20] Daniel: how about model traffic—inference payloads—does that go over the PrivateLink too? any performance hit?
[01:30] Priya: good question. our recommended pattern is control-plane + model artifacts via PrivateLink, and for high-throughput inference we either peer the runtime VPCs or use TGW with VPC endpoints depending on scale. for small pilots an interface endpoint works fine. latency-wise PrivateLink adds minimal overhead—single-digit ms—most variance is from cross-az routing and NAT egress.
[01:55] Alex: yeah and to add, if you colocate runtime in your VPC (Redwood Private managed runtime), you avoid cross-account NAT egress for token/payloads which is the biggest source of tail latency.
[02:10] Samuel: we cannot have any public egress for inference tokens. So endpoint-only is mandatory.
[02:20] Priya: understood. that pushes us to PrivateLink + either Transit Gateway or VPC peering for runtime placement. we should map expected throughput—if you plan sustained hundreds of qps, TGW with dedicated routes is more robust.
[02:35] Maya: our traffic pattern is spiky—peak 400 qps for 1-2 hr windows. avg is 40 qps.
[02:45] Priya: ok that's helpful. batching will smooth spikes—if you batch to tokens-per-request you'll trade off per-request latency for throughput. we'll propose dynamic batching parameters in the pilot.
[02:58] [small crosstalk]
[03:05] Priya: runtime notes: KV cache hit ratio is critical for hot prompts. when cache hits are high, token generation avoids re-computing encoder states and saves tens of ms per token. cold cache or cache misses cause full model passes which expose network and compute latency.
[03:25] Samuel: can you quantify? like if cache hit vs miss, what's the delta?
[03:30] Priya: from our internal tests—on a 70B-class model—cache hits can reduce token latency by ~25-50ms per token depending on sequence length and whether KV is local to the same host. if KV is remote across VPC or through NAT, you add RTT.
[03:50] Alex: and that's why colocating or using same AZ endpoints for runtime matters: keep KV traffic local. also keep an eye on connection setup costs—long lived connections and keepalive reduce TLS handshake overhead.
[04:05] Daniel: about TLS, do you terminate at Redwood side or do we keep mTLS end-to-end? we need assertion in our threat model.
[04:12] Priya: we support mutual TLS for private deployments, and for PrivateLink interface endpoints the TLS is within the VPC but we still recommend mTLS between your services and our runtime endpoints. we can integrate with your SSO for service identities, and Redwood integrates with customer KMS for envelope encryption of model keys.
[04:35] Maya: KMS integration—do you support customer-managed keys (CMK) and HSM-backed keys?
[04:40] Alex: yes, CMK via AWS KMS is supported; for FIPS/HSM we have options to plug customer HSMs in Private deployments. we'll include the exact docs in the security pack.
[04:55] Priya: switching back to networking—NATs are a frequent pain: if your NAT gateway is centralized and we route through it for egress, saturation or cold start queueing can inflate p99 by hundreds ms. we prefer architecture where inference egress is restricted and private endpoints are used instead.
[05:15] Samuel: we can't create outbound to public. so what are the options to reach Redwood without NAT?
[05:22] Priya: two main ones: PrivateLink interface endpoints (preferred) or VPC peering/TGW where you have routes directly into Redwood-managed VPC subnets. PrivateLink is easier for isolation. TGW is better for high-scale interconnects.
[05:40] Maya: DNS—how is service discovery handled? split-horizon? we use Route53 Resolver endpoints.
[05:47] Priya: yes Route53 Resolver + private hosted zones are common—Redwood can provide private DNS records for the interface endpoints. for TGW we rely on peered DNS or resolver endpoints depending on AWS account boundaries. split-horizon can be used to ensure internal names resolve to private IPs only.
[06:05] [pause]
[06:10] Priya: ok runtime perf tradeoffs—batching, kv cache, quantization. batching increases throughput but increases latency per request because we wait to aggregate. we typically expose per-route SLO controls: max batch size, latency cap, and dynamic batching windows.
[06:30] Samuel: for our customer flows, we need p50 < 120ms and p95 < 250ms. is batching acceptable?
[06:38] Priya: yes—if requests are frequent enough to be batched within the latency cap. dynamic batching with small windows (e.g., 10-20ms) can capture microbursts. if traffic is sparse, batching hurts tail; prefix/KV caching helps a lot for that case.
[06:55] Alex: quantization note: int8/4-bit quantization reduces memory and can boost throughput a lot—at cost of some quality drift. for retrieval-assisted prompts and short completions quantization is often fine; for high-fidelity outputs we recommend higher-precision models or eval-led rollouts.
[07:15] Maya: do you have auto rollback on quality regression?
[07:18] Priya: yes, Redwood Optimize integrates eval hooks—you can tie regression alerts to prompt sets; automatic fallback to a higher-precision model variant is supported in rollout policies.
[07:30] Daniel: network MTU or jumbo frame concerns—should we tune anything?
[07:35] Priya: generally not required; RPC payloads are small. but if you have large batch payloads or embeddings with big vectors, increasing MTU can help. more important is keepalive/TCP window tuning for high-throughput connections.
[07:52] [15s silence]
[08:07] Priya: for pilot, we suggest: 1) a small dedicated runtime in your account or connected via PrivateLink, 2) run our benchmark script (we'll share) with your sample traffic patterns, 3) measure p50/p95/p99 latency and tokens/sec, 4) check KV cache hit/miss and adjust TTLs.
[08:28] Alex: and Redwood will log token-level timings, per-route breakdowns and network traces for the pilot so we can correlate network spikes to model stalls.
[08:40] Samuel: about logs and audits—we need full request audit logs and to know which operations touch PII. can you redact or filter?
[08:50] Priya: yes, we support configurable logging and can redact payloads before storage. audit logs include who/when/what model version. for Private deployments logs can be shipped to your SIEM or S3 with customer-controlled retention.
[09:05] Maya: any special routing to reduce inter-AZ hops?
[09:10] Priya: pick same AZ placement where possible, use AZ-aware subnets, and ensure security groups allow AZ-local traffic. cross-AZ routing can add 1-3ms typically, at tail larger.
[09:25] Daniel: can we do eBPF observability or do we have to rely on app-level tracing?
[09:30] Alex: we can provide sidecar traces and also integrate with VPC Flow Logs; for deep packet-level eBPF we'd need additional ops access in Private deployments. we can discuss that in the security pack.
[09:45] [crosstalk]
[09:50] Priya: deployment checklist highlights: subnet sizing (ensure enough IPs for ENIs), route tables for interface endpoints, SG rules for svc ports, NACLs open if needed, resolver endpoints for DNS, and KMS permissions for envelope encryption.
[10:12] Maya: subnet sizing—how many ENIs per runtime instance?
[10:18] Priya: depends on instance/GPU type. we document per-instance ENI counts. for autoscaling clusters you need buffer for burst scaling. a common misconfig is running out of IPs during scale-up which leads to delayed starts and higher tail latency.
[10:35] Samuel: what's the typical onboarding time?
[10:38] Alex: for a pilot with PrivateLink + small runtime, usually 2-4 weeks including security review. if you want TGW or cross-account, add extra for network approvals.
[10:50] Priya: technical deep-dive—latency breakdown: client -> private endpoint (1-5ms), endpoint -> runtime host (0-3ms if same AZ), model forward/back (depends on model & batch size, tens to hundreds ms), token emission network cost (small). so to meet p95 targets we tune batch windows, keep KV warm, and reduce cross-AZ hops.
[11:15] Daniel: about cold starts—do you keep GPUs warm? what's the idle policy?
[11:20] Priya: yes we have warm pool options for Dedicated/Private deployments. you can configure minimum capacity to avoid cold starts; it's a cost/latency tradeoff. for Nimbus given your p95 targets we recommend a small warm pool for peak windows.
[11:35] Alex: question from infra—how do you handle client connection concurrency? single long lived HTTP/2 stream per client is recommended to amortize TLS.
[11:45] Maya: ok that fits our proxy pattern.
[11:48] Priya: also note KB cache eviction policy—LRU-like with TTLs; set your prompt prefixing to maximize cache hits for chatty flows.
[12:00] [brief pause]
[12:05] Priya: perf benchmarking details we'll share: scripted QPS profile, synthetic prompt shapes, sequence length distributions, and a KV warmup harness. measure: p50/p95/p99 latency, tokens/sec, effective batch sizes, KV hit ratio, and network RTT distributions.
[12:25] Samuel: will you be able to run bench with our sample dataset? some prompts include long instructions (~700 tokens).
[12:32] Priya: yes we'll parameterize sequence lengths; long instructions emphasize memory/kv pressure and quantization impact. we'll run both quantized and fp16 variants.
[12:45] Daniel: security: SAML/SCIM SSO for team access?
[12:50] Alex: supported, we'll include SSO, role-based access, and audit logging in the security pack. for Private deployments you can use your IdP via SAML and SCIM for provisioning.
[13:05] Maya: one more—do you support egress whitelisting with static IPs?
[13:10] Priya: yes—we can allocate static egress IPs (NAT or pooled egress) for outbound services. for no-public-egress usage we route via PrivateLink and avoid egress.
[13:22] [small chuckle]
[13:25] Alex: okay next, let's talk example rollback: if quantized model shows a 2% drop on a key eval set we'll automatically fail over to the non-quantized variant while we investigate.
[13:40] Priya: ops note: keep an eye on kernel selection and torch/cuda driver compatibility—those affect latency more than you'd expect when we change instance types. we'll validate with your AMI/kernel matrix during pilot.
[13:58] Maya: in terms of observability, we need traces correlated with network logs. what do you provide?
[14:05] Priya: token-level timings (synthesis vs nll vs kv fetch), per-request trace ids, and you can pull logs or push to SIEM; we also provide per-route dashboards in Redwood Console.
[14:20] Samuel: ok what are the immediate actions after this call?
[14:24] Alex: we'll share the benchmark script, security pack, and a short pilot runbook. we'll also need a VPC diagram and contact for network approvals.
[14:35] Priya: one more caution—if you use centralized proxy stacks that rewrite headers or terminate TLS you need to ensure trace propagation headers are preserved, otherwise the token-level timing will be incomplete.
[14:50] Daniel: noted.
[14:55] [end recap]
[15:00] Alex: recap: Redwood to send security docs + perf scripts; customer to share VPC/subnet/CIDR/NAT details; schedule pilot week of 2027-08-30; next sync after initial bench.
[15:18] Samuel: sounds good. thanks everyone.
[15:22] Priya: thanks, bye.
